content: The databases were searched comprehensively, and the review included 94 trials with a total of 9,821 participants. From these, three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 240 participants were selected for inclusion in this scope review based on population criteria. These trials were conducted by authors from Japan and the USA. The participants in these studies either reported functional limitations or were classified as frail. The mean age of participants ranged from 70 to 74 years, with sample sizes varying between 49 and 132 participants. The exercise interventions lasted between 8 and 24 weeks. One trial utilized progressive resistance exercise, another employed multimodal exercise, and the third focused on T’ai Chi. Liu and Latham (2009) conducted a Cochrane systematic review to evaluate the effects of progressive resistance strength training on physical function in older adults. The Cochrane Bone, Joint, and Muscle Trauma Group database (up to March 2007), CENTRAL (2007, Issue 2), MEDLINE (1966 to May 2008), EMBASE (1980 to February 2007), CINAHL (1982 to July 2007), and two other electronic databases were searched. Although their review included 121 RCTs with 6,700 participants, only 10 trials were initially included in this scope review. One trial was excluded due to irrelevant outcomes, leaving nine trials (715 participants) for further analysis. These trials were conducted by authors from Australia, the Netherlands, New Zealand, the UK, and the USA. Participants in these studies had physical performance limitations, difficulty rising from a chair, or weak leg muscle strength. The mean age of participants ranged from 71 to 81 years, with sample sizes between 16 and 243 participants. Exercise durations ranged from 8 to 25 weeks, with six trials lasting 12 weeks or less. The World Health Organization (WHO) updated this review in 2015, incorporating two additional trials into the evidence synthesis. Van Abbema et al. (2015) conducted a meta-analysis to assess the effects of exercise on gait speed in older adults. Studies published between 1990 and 2013 were searched in PubMed, EMBASE, EBSCO (including AMED, CINAHL, ERIC, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and SocINDEX), and the Cochrane Library. Their review included 25 trials with 2,389 participants. After removing ineligible and duplicate studies, three trials (226 participants) were added to this scope review. The lead authors of these trials were from Spain, Japan, or Australia. Participants were either frail or had geriatric syndromes or balance concerns. All three trials employed multimodal exercise interventions lasting 3 to 6 months. Burton et al. (2015) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the effects of exercise programs on reducing falls in older adults with dementia. Studies published between January 2000 and February 2010 were searched in PubMed, MEDLINE (ProQuest), PsycINFO, EMBASE, CINAHL, and Scopus. Four trials (336 participants) were included in their review. After excluding ineligible trials, two trials from Finland and Australia (250 participants with mean ages of 78 and 82 years, respectively) were added to this scope review. Both trials utilized multimodal exercise interventions lasting 6 to 12 months. One trial delivered group-based or home-based exercise, while the other trial implemented an individualized exercise program. Forbes et al. conducted a search in 2013 using databases such as PubMed, MEDLINE, and Web of Science. Two trials (67 participants) were added to this scope review. These trials were conducted by authors from Australia and the USA, with mean participant ages of 74 and 75 years, respectively. Both trials employed multimodal exercise interventions lasting 12 weeks or 4 months. One trial (Steinberg et al., 2009) was excluded from the final effect-size calculation due to missing post-test mean and standard deviation data. Pitkäla et al. (2013) conducted a systematic review to evaluate the effects of physical exercise on mobility and physical functioning in older adults with dementia. Studies published through August 31, 2011, were searched in databases such as PubMed, the Cochrane Library, the Cochrane Database of Abstracts of Reviews of Effects (DARE), CINAHL, and Nursing@Ovid. Twenty RCTs (1,378 participants) were included in the review. Nine trials from France, Israel, Korea, and the UK were added to this review. All trials utilized multimodal exercise interventions lasting between 2 weeks and 12 months. The WHO ICOP guidelines systematically reviewed the effects of physical exercise on older adults with limitations in activities of daily living (ADLs). Progressive resistance training was compared with control groups, and the evidence was graded. The review found low-quality evidence for the effect of progressive resistance exercise on increasing muscle strength and very low-quality evidence for improving chair stand performance. Multimodal exercise showed moderate-quality evidence for improving muscle strength, balance, and chair stand performance, as well as low-quality evidence for improving overall physical function. T’ai Chi demonstrated low-quality evidence for improving balance. Adverse events, such as muscle soreness and joint pain, were commonly reported and potentially related to exercise. Severe adverse events, including fractures, hospitalizations, or deaths, were infrequently reported, and their relationship to exercise was unclear.
